reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: An abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that bypasses the capillary bed, creating a right-to-left shunt
The majority are associated with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease), so a positive family history and mucocutaneous telangiectasia are important clues
Presents with breathlessness, hypoxaemia, and sometimes cyanosis, digital clubbing, or haemoptysis, though many are found incidentally
Classic physiological signs are platypnoea and orthodeoxia - breathlessness and desaturation on standing that improve when lying down - reflecting basal predominance of the lesions
The lost capillary filter permits paradoxical embolism, causing stroke, transient ischaemic attack, and brain abscess even in patients with only mild respiratory symptoms
Contrast (bubble) echocardiography is a sensitive screening test for the right-to-left shunt, with CT pulmonary angiography defining the anatomy
Transcatheter embolisation is the treatment of choice for lesions of significant size to abolish the shunt and reduce embolic risk
Patients require antibiotic prophylaxis for procedures and meticulous care with intravenous lines to prevent air or septic emboli reaching the systemic circulation
reference.pathophysiology: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation is a thin-walled vascular sac or tangle connecting a feeding pulmonary artery directly to a draining pulmonary vein without an intervening capillary network. Blood shunted through this communication is not oxygenated and bypasses the capillary filter, producing hypoxaemia that worsens with increased basal blood flow on standing (orthodeoxia). Loss of the filtering capillary bed allows thrombi and bacteria to pass into the systemic arterial circulation, causing paradoxical embolic stroke and cerebral abscess. Most lesions are congenital and part of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia; the fragile vessels can also rupture and bleed.
additionalDifferentials: Intracardiac right-to-left shunt (e.g. patent foramen ovale, atrial septal defect)
Other causes of chronic hypoxaemia and cyanosis
Solitary pulmonary nodule of other aetiology on imaging
additionalInvestigations: Contrast (agitated saline bubble) echocardiography to detect a right-to-left shunt
CT pulmonary angiography to map feeding and draining vessels
Pulse oximetry and shunt-fraction measurement, including postural (standing versus supine) assessment
Screening and genetic evaluation for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, including family members
Brain imaging if neurological symptoms suggest paradoxical embolism or abscess
redFlags: Neurological symptoms indicating paradoxical embolic stroke, transient ischaemic attack, or brain abscess - an emergency requiring urgent evaluation
Haemoptysis or haemothorax from lesion rupture, which can be massive and life-threatening
Pregnancy, during which lesions can enlarge and bleed and shunting can worsen
reference.prognosis: With embolisation the shunt and embolic risk are markedly reduced and prognosis is good, though lesions can recur or recanalise and new ones may develop over time, so long-term surveillance is needed, particularly in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
pitfalls: Attributing hypoxaemia to cardiac or parenchymal disease and missing an intrapulmonary shunt
Failing to screen for and counsel about paradoxical embolism and brain abscess risk
Not implementing air-embolism precautions for intravenous access and procedures
Overlooking hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and the need for family screening
